Chapter 4: Storytelling, Truth, and the Struggle to Make Sense.
You know, everyone tells stories—sometimes to themselves, sometimes to others—all in an effort to make sense of the world. But here’s the thing: stories are slippery. They can comfort us, twist reality, or open our eyes, depending on who’s telling them and why.
After the Langley trial, the law student noticed something surprising. The stories people told about the case—and even about their own lives—turned out to be just as important as the cold, hard facts.
The courtroom? It felt like a stage. Everyone was playing a part. Prosecutors cast Langley as a real threat, someone who needed to be locked away for good. The defense, on the other hand, tried to show him as a product of his environment—a man let down by everyone around him. And the victim’s family... they shared their own heartbreaking story. One of loss, of grief, of a life that could never be replaced.
But underneath all those public versions, there were quieter stories—ones that didn't quite fit the neat categories of good or evil. The more the law student dug into the case, the more tangled things became. Facts, memories, interviews, transcripts—they all started to blend together, weaving a tapestry that was both haunting and, in its own way, beautiful.
Most of us want to believe that the truth is out there, just waiting to be found. But the reality? Truth often depends on where you're standing. The law student realized that every story told in court was shaped by the person telling it—their needs, their fears, their hopes. And honestly, isn’t that the same with the stories we tell ourselves about childhood, family, or the past?
Trying to write—and rewrite—these stories became a kind of survival tool. It was a way to bring order to a world that could feel overwhelming. But it also served as a reminder: no story is ever really finished. There are always gaps, moments that don’t quite fit, and contradictions we can’t resolve.
